newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - Q4 ECI to shape the week.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - Q4 ECI to shape the week.

text.p: The release of the U.S. fourth quarter Employment Cost Index (ECI) on Tuesday will shape the market's landscape in the coming week, bond analysts said.

"The Employment Cost Index is the most significant feature," said John Williams, managing director and chief global markets economist at Bankers Trust. "It's the most important price statistic since the Crusades."
After the ECI on Tuesday, the statistic of most interest to the market is the fourth-quarter GDP (Gross Domestic Product) figure, analysts said.
According to a Reuters poll, economists, on average, are forecasting a 0.9 percent rise in the fourth-quarter ECI and a strong, 3.9 percent expansion in fourth-quarter GDP.
But market strategists said the ECI's behavior would be the most influential, with the potential to shape the market's performance for the rest of the week.

"The Employment Cost Index is really going to be the big one," said William Hornbarger, fixed-income strategist at AG Edwards & Sons Inc. "The ECI has been the mantra of the market this week and last week. Wage inflation is the No. 1 topic on the market's mind right now."

The reason for that is that the ECI has always been the best measure of employment costs and, because labor accounts for two-thirds of the cost of producing goods, is the best inflation gauge available, said Williams.
But the ECI acquired its current prominence in the market after Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan referred to it in his Humphrey-Hawkins Congressional testimony in last July.

"Until Greenspan mentioned it in July, the markets ignored it and focused on much less reliable inflation measures," said Williams. "Now that Greenspan has educated the market, the ECI is extremely topical."
If the ECI rise is more moderate than expected, a strong GDP number on Friday would not be likely to throw the market off balance, analysts said.

"I don't think the GDP data by themselves will swing too many votes or opinions, especially if trade is a big factor in the strength," said Matthew Alexy, chief market strategist at Credit Suisse First Boston.
On the other hand, "a very small move in the ECI can cause a big move in interest rates," Alexy said.
If the ECI rose just 0.7 percent, the 30-year bond yield could fall 15 basis points, he said.
If the ECI rises 1.0 percent, the benchmark Treasury 30-year bond yield could rise 15 basis points, Alexy said.
In late trade on Friday, the 30-year Treasury bond was trading at 95-3/32, down 12/32 to yield 6.89 percent.
On Wednesday, the Treasury's new 10-year inflation-indexed bond will have its debut auction.

"The first auction should go decently to maybe something slightly better than decent," said Hornbarger. "There will be people out there interested in the bonds and the Treasury set it at a good size that will be digestable for the market."

Besides the fourth-quarter ECI and GDP readings, the market will also get December existing homes figures, forecast at an annualized rate of 4.0 million, two weekly reports on store sales, and the Conference Board's January consumer confidence index -- forecast at 112.0 vs. 113.8 in December.
December durable goods orders, due on Wednesday, are forecast at up 1.2 percent, after a 1.6 percent November drop.

The Conference Board's December Help-Wanted Index is due on Thursday and on Friday, when the session starts out with the release of Q4 GDP, the market will also get the January Chicago Purchasing Managers report, December new home sales and the final January University of Michigan's consumer sentiment survey.
Dealers indicated that Federal funds would open between 5-1/4 percent and 5-5/16 percent on Monday.
